turns.en: You recently wrote about four buckets of styles of investing that might be applied, called adventure. Private market tech, what's called? Can you enumerate those and just like say a sentence on heck of an H?
turns.zh: 你最近写了一篇文章，讲可以套用到私募市场科技投资上的四种投资风格，好像叫『冒险』（adventure）之类的？你能把这几种列举一下，每种简单说一句话吗？

turns.en: I'm just in this point in my career. I've been there for a decade. I've had hundreds of deals that I sit in these discussions, and I just realize people aren't communicating very well. Did this exercise where I'm like, what are the mindsets people bring to investing?
turns.zh: 我只是走到了职业生涯的这个节点。我在这行已经待了十年，经手过几百笔交易，参加过无数次这样的讨论，我就是意识到，大家其实没在好好沟通。于是我做了这么一个练习：人们做投资时，到底带着怎样的心态？

turns.en: I think there's basically four types of mindsets. The one that we were talking about before is like this traditional finance mindset, which is the correct proxy for the health of a business is the market it's going into and its finances.
turns.zh: 我觉得基本上有四种心态。我们刚才聊的那一种是传统的金融心态，认为衡量一家公司健康程度的正确代理指标（proxy），是它所在的市场和它的财务数据。

turns.en: What are the SaaS metrics? What is the size of the market? And that is a proxy for the entire business. So that's what clearly growth investors did this, but like more and more you see early stage series A people do this, which to me is a little bit discorded.
turns.zh: SaaS 指标是什么？市场有多大？这些就被当成整门生意的代理指标。所以成长期投资人（growth investors）显然是这么做的，但你会看到越来越多早期、A 轮（Series A）阶段的人也这么干，这在我看来有点错位。

turns.en: Then there's what I call productive investors, which you believe you're investing in a productive asset and the productive asset is what's creating value. And if you believe in that as it creates value, it will create market. And as it creates value, you're going to have to find ways for the business to catch up to that value.
turns.zh: 然后是我所说的生产性投资人（productive investors）：你相信自己投的是一项生产性资产，是这项资产在创造价值。如果你相信它创造价值，它就会创造出市场。而随着它创造价值，你得想办法让这门生意追上那份价值。

turns.en: And so the type of diligence you do if you're a productive investor is more like, what is the technical approach? What are the adjacent markets? How fast is this like we do evolve? How close is it to a capturing value? Like that sort of stuff. Is this the right team to build it?
turns.zh: 所以，作为一个生产性投资人，你要做的尽调更像是：技术路径是什么？相邻市场有哪些？这东西演化得有多快？它离捕获价值有多近？诸如此类。这是不是能把事情做成的正确团队？

turns.en: Then there's what I call frontier investing. I think this is the romantic idealized version of VC from like the 60s and 70s, which is kind of yellow. Like founders know better than VCs and they've seen something that I don't see and they're going to go out there and do it and like, who am I to second guess them?
turns.zh: 然后是我所说的前沿投资（frontier investing）。我觉得这是那种源自六、七十年代、被浪漫化、理想化的风险投资（VC）版本，基本上就是 YOLO（放手一搏）。就像创始人比 VC 更懂，他们看到了我没看到的东西，他们要出去干一番，我又凭什么去质疑他们？

turns.en: And they almost like talent networks, right? Like I would say critics. And I mean, remember when he was investing in new tropics, he invested in soil and he invested in Oculus, he invested in Coinbase and in crypto.
turns.zh: 他们几乎就像人才网络，对吧？我是说……我是说，还记得他当年做投资的时候吗，他投了 Anthropic，投了 Sol，投了 Oculus，投了 Coinbase，也投了加密货币。

turns.en: I mean, it's like every science fiction trope from the 70s and 80s, you kind of invest in and you just don't overthink any of these things. So it's almost like this strong form of the productive. And then the last one and it is always so surprising how prevalent it is is speculative investors. They don't even care about the asset.
turns.zh: 我是说，简直就是把七、八十年代的每一个科幻桥段都投了个遍，而且你根本不会去过度思考这些东西。所以这几乎是生产性投资的一种强化版。然后最后一种——它的普遍程度总是让我吃惊——就是投机性投资人（speculative investors）。他们甚至不在乎那项资产本身。

turns.en: They just want to time a market. You'll see this like in crypto and in the secondary markets. They don't know about the underlying asset. They probably don't even know about the actual business metrics.
turns.zh: 他们只是想给市场择时（time a market）。你会在加密货币和二级市场（secondary markets）里看到这种。他们不了解底层资产，甚至可能连实际的经营指标都不清楚。

turns.en: But they're like, well, this looks cheap. It's clearly going to go up in value. Oh, this is the top of the market. You know, like I'm going to get out. They're trying to like time markets. They're actually just doing speculative. They're not really interested in like, will the business grow?
turns.zh: 但他们就是，『嗯，这看起来很便宜，价值明显会涨。哦，这是市场顶部了，你知道吧，我要撤了。』他们想给市场择时。他们其实就是在做投机。他们并不真的关心这门生意会不会增长。

turns.en: And again, the problem is is if you have all of these art types, you can justify any deal or not justify any deals. If you don't know what your beliefs are, you'll always justify whatever personal bias you have. If you think about yourself as a productive investor focused on, I love this idea that disruptive technologies.
turns.zh: 再说一遍，问题在于，如果你把这些五花八门的类型全都混在一起，你就能给任何一笔交易找到理由，或者不给任何交易找理由。如果你不知道自己的信念是什么，你永远都会去为个人的偏见辩护。如果你把自己定位成一个生产性投资人，专注于——我很喜欢这个说法——颠覆性技术（disruptive technologies）。

turns.en: You should not look at some of these traditional things that so many investors talk about. Talk about what you do look at. Like you look at so many companies. What is your method by which to assess whether or not someone might be creating a truly disruptive piece of technology, a valuable asset?
turns.zh: 那你就不该去看那么多投资人挂在嘴边的传统指标。说说你到底看什么吧。你看过这么多公司，你用什么方法来判断某个人是不是在创造一项真正颠覆性的技术、一项有价值的资产？

turns.en: So I only do computer science and testing and I only do infrastructure investing and I think infrastructure as an industry has a certain shape. Certain buying behaviors, the technology looks a certain way in the industry acts a certain way.
turns.zh: 所以我只做计算机科学那一套，我只做基础设施（infrastructure）投资。我认为基础设施作为一个行业，有它特定的形态、特定的采购行为，技术呈现出特定的样子，行业也有特定的运作方式。

turns.en: And so what you're trying to do is you're trying to take a technical approach and you're trying to map it into that technostrategic framework. And the way you do that, there's a number of approaches. One of them you're like, what are the leading companies doing internally?
turns.zh: 所以你要做的，是拿一种技术路径，去把它映射进那个『技术—战略』框架里。做法有很多种。其中一种是：领先的公司内部在做什么？

turns.en: And this will give you a glimpse on maybe this is how platforms evolve. Or perhaps the team that is doing this didn't it another context and now they're actually bringing it to this context. I think it's one of these things where like how much can you diligence without actually just using the numbers for a proxy?
turns.zh: 这能让你瞥见，也许平台就是这样演化的。又或者，正在做这件事的团队，曾在别的场景里做过它，如今把它带到了这个场景里。我觉得这是那种『在不直接拿数字当代理指标的情况下，你到底能做多少尽调』的问题。

turns.en: You can talk to customers will they use this? You can see if there's like adjacent budgets that are growing that could argue will fragment to become this. Or maybe you have early signs of willingness to pay but they actually haven't figured out the business model.
turns.zh: 你可以去问客户，他们会不会用这个？你可以看看有没有正在增长的相邻预算，可以论证它会分裂出来变成这个东西。又或者，你也许已经看到早期付费意愿的信号，但他们其实还没想清楚商业模式。

turns.en: I was thinking every tech wave, you know, been in the industry for 30 ways, every tech wave. People like hand ring about margins. I can't remember for the cloud. I remember from over I remember for the internet clearly now people worry about margins. So maybe you're like, there's a willingness to pay.
turns.zh: 我一直在想，每一波科技浪潮——你知道，我在这行待了三十年，每一波科技浪潮，人们都会为利润率（margins）捶胸顿足。云的那波我不太记得了，我记得……互联网的那波我印象很深，如今人们又在担心利润率。所以也许你会想，付费意愿是有的。

turns.en: And there's a lot of interest but we haven't figured out the cogs yet in the actual viable business model. So like you're using partial indicators not full indicators in order to do this. And so my team is a lot of technical people, product people, many have PhDs.
turns.zh: 也有大量的兴趣，但我们还没搞清楚销货成本（COGS）和真正可行的商业模式。所以你是在用一些局部指标、而不是完整指标来做这件事。我的团队里有很多技术人、产品人，很多人有博士学位（PhD）。

turns.en: We don't second guess the tech like the founder will know the tech better than us but we can't ask the question, how does this tech fit into the bottom platforms fit into spending? How does this tech fit in with our understanding of stickiness and defensibility?
turns.zh: 我们不会去质疑技术本身——创始人对技术的理解肯定比我们强——但我们可以问：这项技术怎么嵌进底层平台、嵌进开支里？这项技术跟我们对于粘性（stickiness）和防御性（defensibility）的理解怎么契合？

turns.en: And then we look at early market numbers and we'll say, hey listen, a financial investor would puket this but it actually shows that the customers are really interested to figure something out and will they be able to figure something out? So there's a lot of diligence you can do.
turns.zh: 然后我们看早期的市场数据，我们会说，嘿，听着，一个财务型投资人看到这个会想吐，但它其实说明客户是真有兴趣去把某个东西搞明白——而他们能不能搞明白？所以你能做相当多的尽调。

turns.en: We're with frontier investing. I don't think you do any of that. It's people, is this the best team to do this crazy thing and then you just yellow? You were saying before we hit start that nobody understands network effects. Can you explain what you meant? I've realized that even the most common terms you use, there's no consensus on.
turns.zh: 而到了前沿投资，我觉得你这些都不做。就是看人，看这是不是做这件疯狂之事的最佳团队，然后你就 YOLO 一把。你在我们开始录之前说，没人真正理解网络效应（network effects），你能解释一下是什么意思吗？我意识到，就连我们最常用的那些术语，其实都谈不上有共识。

turns.en: And so for example, network effects is the favorite one that I pick up. I asked you before. I messed it up. No, you didn't mess it up. You said what like a third of people say. So I said, so what is a network effect? And what did you say? I said a product that gets better as it adds a marginally user. Right.
turns.zh: 所以举个例子，网络效应是我最爱挑的一个词。我之前问过你。我把它搞砸了。不，你没搞砸。你说的其实是大概三分之一的人会说的定义。所以我说，那到底什么是网络效应？你当时怎么说的？我说，一个每增加一个边际用户就会变得更好的产品。对。

turns.en: So to me, this is almost a top logical definition because most products will get better as you add a user, right? They will find a bug. They will provide feedback. They will tell other people that doesn't say anything about defensibility.
turns.zh: 所以对我来说，这几乎是个拓扑学式（topological）的定义，因为大多数产品在你增加用户时都会变好，对吧？他们会发现一个 bug，会给你反馈，会告诉别人——这其实说明不了任何关于防御性的东西。

turns.en: But other people when they use the term network effects, they actually mean the original meaning of the term network effect from the 70s, which is a telephone network. Where when users join, they interact with each other that grows super linearly. And that's where you get like natural monopolies.
turns.zh: 但另一些人用『网络效应』这个词时，他们其实指的是这个词在七十年代的原始含义，也就是电话网络。用户加入后会彼此互动，互动量随人数超线性（super-linearly）增长。这才是你得到天然垄断（natural monopolies）的地方。

turns.en: And other people use the term network effect more to be like an actual flywheel, so like a self reinforcing flywheel. So not just like things get better, but like it's self reinforces in some sort of a way. This where you hear the term like data network effects.
turns.zh: 还有人用『网络效应』这个词，更多是指一个真正的飞轮（flywheel），也就是一个自我强化的飞轮。不只是东西会变好，而是它以某种方式自我强化。这就是你会听到『数据网络效应』（data network effects）这个说法的地方。

turns.en: But even in that sense, like you don't know if that self reinforcement is super linear or not. So you don't know if it makes it defensible or not. So you have this very common word that's on 70% of pitch decks where a founder is sitting in front to hit pitch. And nobody has consensus on what it means. And so how are you to find it?
turns.zh: 但即便在那个意义上，你也不知道那种自我强化是不是超线性的。所以你不知道它到底能不能带来防御性。于是你就有了这么一个非常常见的词，出现在 70% 的商业计划书（pitch deck）里，创始人坐在投资人面前做路演，可没人对它的含义有共识。那你要怎么据此判断呢？

turns.en: So I think the root of the confusion is not a definitional problem. I think the root of the confusion is conceptually we conflate the mechanism with the shape of the moat. There's many things that could create a moat, right? Like a brand scale, a two-sided marketplace network effect.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，这种混淆的根源不是定义问题。我认为根源在于，我们在概念上把『机制』和『护城河（moat）的形状』混为一谈了。有很多东西都能造出护城河，对吧？比如品牌、规模、双边市场、网络效应。

turns.en: But that moat, to reason about that, is only really useful if it has some properties that makes the company defensible against somebody else. If that moat grows super linearly with scale, like a classic Metcalf Swann network effect, wood, that's really defensible. If it grows sub-linearly with scale, it may not be useful at all.
turns.zh: 但那条护城河，你要去推理它，只有当它具备某些属性、能让公司抵御别人时，才真的有用。如果那条护城河随规模超线性增长，就像经典的梅特卡夫定律（Metcalfe's Law）式网络效应那样，那它就非常有防御性。如果它随规模亚线性（sub-linearly）增长，那它可能压根没用。

turns.en: And so I think to you and I have a conversation of defensibility, I think the first thing we need to do is not conflate the shape of the moat within mechanism that caused it. So first, I think we should say the moat that we have is super linear, it's linear, or it's sub-linear with scale.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，你我要聊防御性，第一件事就是不要把护城河的形状和造成它的机制混为一谈。所以首先，我们应该说清楚：我们手上的这条护城河，随规模是超线性、线性，还是亚线性的。

turns.en: And then the second thing, a lot of things actually contribute to a moat. For example, like we mentioned network effects will or scale effect. What's a scale effect? The scale effect, the scale effect, to me, is as the company scale, it can reduce unit economics normally because it has pricing power.
turns.zh: 然后第二件事，很多东西其实都在为护城河做贡献。比如我们提到的网络效应，或者规模效应（scale effect）。规模效应是什么？对我来说，规模效应就是随着公司规模扩大，它能降低单位经济（unit economics），通常是因为它有了定价权（pricing power）。

turns.en: For example, or maybe CAQ goes down because of brand. What's a two-sided marketplace that's very different to me than a network effect? That's where basically you've got self-inforcing supply and demand.
turns.zh: 举个例子，又或者获客成本（CAC）因为品牌而下降。那双边市场（two-sided marketplace）呢？这在我看来跟网络效应很不一样。双边市场基本上是你有了自我强化的供给和需求。

turns.en: So I think that there are many mechanisms, and then there's the shape, and then to have a discussion, I think you want to make sure that the shape is something that actually provides long-term defensibility.
turns.zh: 所以我认为，机制有很多种，然后还有形状，而要展开讨论，我觉得你得确保那个形状是真正能提供长期防御性的东西。

turns.en: And the last thing I'll say is it's almost impossible to have these conversations in isolation because we're actually talking about competitive equilibrium. Because if you have a network effect, then namely the competitor has a network effect too.
turns.zh: 最后我想说的是，几乎不可能孤立地进行这些讨论，因为我们其实是在谈竞争均衡（competitive equilibrium）。因为如果你有网络效应，那么说白了，你的竞争对手也有网络效应。

turns.en: And maybe if they have more capital than you can grow faster, that probably impacts the shape of your moat. You may not grow as fast marginally because they're stealing your customers or something like that.
turns.zh: 也许如果他们的资本比你多、能增长得更快，那大概率会影响你护城河的形状。你在边际上可能就没法增长得那么快，因为他们在抢你的客户之类的。

turns.en: And so I just think that we need a very, very basic concept, we need to not conflate the notion of the actual shape with the actual mechanism. And then I think we should enumerate the mechanisms because something like the definition that you had just doesn't really help anybody.
turns.zh: 所以我就是觉得，我们需要一个非常非常基础的概念：不要把『实际的形状』和『实际的机制』混为一谈。然后我觉得我们应该把这些机制逐一列举出来，因为像你刚才那种定义，其实帮不到任何人。

turns.en: But I actually think defenseability in most is not really even worth talking about most of the time. Let me explain why. Here's my experience for what it's worth. turns.zh: 但我其实觉得，防御性和护城河在大多数时候根本不太值得讨论。让我解释一下为什么。以下是我的经验，姑且一听。如果你投的市场在增长，那么公司之间是不会想去竞争的。会有很多新的空白地带（white space）被创造出来。

turns.zh: 所以它们会试图做的，就是直接挪进其他空白地带。如果市场在增长，谈防御性其实是第二、第三位的事情。而如果市场在放缓或萎缩，通常不管有没有护城河，它都会走向整合（consolidate）。

turns.en: It'll never occur value. It's not defensible. That's fine. But as long as the market's growing in a large market, it's going to occur a lot of value. I remember this about the neoclouds. turns.zh: 它永远不会创造价值，它没有防御性。那没关系。但只要市场在增长、而且是个大市场，它就会创造大量价值。我对那些新云（neoclouds）也是这个印象。有人说它永远不……收入质量差。我觉得我们作为投资人，有点被『用防御性来思考』这件事给骗了。

turns.en: How would you describe the state of the union today in your world in infrastructure like obviously it's changing really, really fast. There's new kinds of companies, but there do seem to be some layers or some categories. Yeah, how would you describe what it looks like today?
turns.zh: 你会怎么描述你所在领域——基础设施——今天的『国情咨文』（state of the union）？显然它变化得非常非常快，出现了新型的公司，但似乎确实有一些层次或者说类别。你会怎么描述它今天的样子？

turns.en: Yeah, so for me, the definition of infrastructure is like the differentiation is actually technical, where I don't view SaaS or apps as that way. If you invest in a SaaS or apps company, it's like a technical investment, it's like a business model innovation.
turns.zh: 对我来说，基础设施的定义，其区分点其实是技术性的，我不会把 SaaS 或应用（apps）看成那样。如果你投一家 SaaS 或应用公司，那不算技术投资，而更像是一种商业模式创新。

turns.en: So because for us as a technical innovation, it has to sit kind of in the traditional technical stack. So the traditional technical stack for infrastructure is compute, network, storage, and databases, right? And each one of those has a sub components and they all have buyers. We're seeing that being kind of reformed with AI a bit.
turns.zh: 所以对我们来说，作为一项技术创新，它必须坐在传统的技术栈里。基础设施的传统技术栈就是计算（compute）、网络（network）、存储（storage）和数据库（databases），对吧？每一块都有子组件，也都有对应的买家。我们看到这些正在被 AI 重塑。

turns.en: And so all of them are being disrupted, but also now you have models which I would consider infrastructure. They look to me more like A6 than they look like traditional software. I mean, like the capital needs, the competitive pressures on them. And then I think they're disrupting the entire application stack above them.
turns.zh: 所以它们全都在被颠覆，但与此同时，你现在还多了模型（models），我也会把模型算作基础设施。它们在我看来更像是资本密集型的东西，而不像传统软件——我是说，看它们的资本需求、它们承受的竞争压力。而且我觉得它们正在颠覆其上的整个应用栈。

turns.en: Like we don't even know if they will layer. I mean, maybe you could argue with Jeff, you can kind of put them in software, but traditionally they're their own separate entity that you can't marry to software very well.
turns.zh: 我们甚至不知道它们会不会分层（layer）。我是说，也许你可以跟 Jeff 争一下，你多少能把它们归进软件里，但传统上它们是自成一体的独立实体，你没法很好地把它跟软件绑在一起。

turns.en: And so I would say we're in kind of a point of maximum disruption, but all of the infrastructure supporting software, whether it's five-coded or not, or whether it's to build models or not. I mean, that doesn't change like the major components. So I think we do have a bit of a traditional mindset of compute, network, storage, databases.
turns.zh: 所以我会说，我们正处在一个颠覆最大化的节点上，但所有支撑软件的基础设施——不管它是不是被 vibe coding（氛围编程）出来的，也不管它是不是用来训练模型的——那些主要组件其实并没有变。所以我觉得我们确实还是有点传统思维定式：计算、网络、存储、数据库。

turns.en: But we also throw up our hands and like, this is all changing so fast. Because for example, when you're worried about dev tooling in the past, you're worried about ergonomics for a human. And I don't really worry about that.
turns.zh: 但我们也会两手一摊说，这一切变得太快了。因为举个例子，过去你担心开发工具（dev tooling）时，你担心的是给人的工效学（ergonomics）。而这一点我其实不太担心了。

turns.en: And then actually a lot of the design decisions that we made as technologists were like, well, a human's going to be using this so it can't be too complicated. And then you would trade off things like safety or you trade off things like reliability. Well, you don't really have to do that anymore because the models are doing it.
turns.zh: 而且实际上，我们作为技术人做的很多设计决策都是，嗯，这东西是给人用的，所以不能太复杂。然后你就会在安全性上做取舍，或者在可靠性上做取舍。可现在你其实不必再这么做了，因为是模型在用它。

turns.en: So I think this is kind of the biggest refresh of computer science infrastructure. We've seen maybe since the internet, maybe forever. Would the shorthand for this be that each of those five portions of infrastructure are being refactored for agents? Is that overly simplifying? So I split it into two pieces.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，这大概是计算机科学基础设施自互联网以来、甚至也许是有史以来最大的一次刷新。这事儿的简版说法，是不是说基础设施的这五个部分每一个都在为智能体（agents）做重构？这么说是不是太简化了？我会把它拆成两块。

turns.en: People are vibe coding a lot of stuff. There's most software being written never before, and that stuff has to run somewhere. That's not agents. That's just normal software. turns.zh: 人们正在 vibe coding 出很多东西。有史以来最多的软件正在被写出来，而这些东西得跑在某个地方。那不是智能体，那就是普通软件。也许是一个智能体创造了它，也许是一个人创造了它，但它需要数据库，需要算力。所以这是一件事。

turns.en: It's like the product of agents. And then the other one is like we're building these new systems that have AI at the heart of them. And then how does that change it? Those are the two. So just assume way more software being built and has to be run and deployed somewhere.
turns.zh: 这算是智能体的产物。另一件是，我们在搭建这些以 AI 为核心的新系统，那又会带来什么改变？就这两件事。所以你就假设会有多得多的软件被构建出来，而且必须在某个地方被运行和部署。

turns.en: And then think that now we also have systems that actually create agents. It seems like each new wave of technology, there's a new kind of database that's needed. Are you seeing that across all the areas that you care about that because of AI? There's whole new entrance? Yeah, I think so.
turns.zh: 然后再想想，我们现在还有了能真正创造智能体的系统。似乎每一波新技术，都会需要一种新的数据库。在你关心的所有这些领域里，你是不是都看到因为 AI 而冒出了全新的进入者（entrants）？是的，我觉得是这样。

turns.en: I mean, I think a lot of infrastructure is getting a bit sleepy. And now because agents are very sophisticated, that's no longer the case. So for example, let's take OLTP. What is OLTP? OLTP is a transaction database. I think the oracles of the world. That's a pretty mature industry. You didn't see a lot of movement.
turns.zh: 我是说，我觉得很多基础设施都有点变得昏昏欲睡了。而现在因为智能体非常老练，这种情况不再成立了。举个例子，就拿 OLTP 来说。什么是 OLTP？OLTP 就是事务型数据库（transaction database）。我觉得像 Oracle 那些。那是个相当成熟的行业，你看不到多少动静。

turns.en: Maybe you saw like movement to the cloud or something like that. But now we're seeing really interesting companies that are like, you know what? The hard thing about using a database from a programmer standpoint is that databases always have their own languages. And they've had their own languages for technical reasons.
turns.zh: 也许你看到过向云的迁移之类的。但现在我们看到一些非常有意思的公司，它们说，你知道吗？从程序员的角度看，用数据库最难的地方在于，数据库总是有它们自己的语言。而且因为技术原因，它们一直有自己的语言。

turns.en: And it's really, really hard to have them work with normal programming languages. And one of the reasons is if you change that language, like anybody that knows the databases wouldn't know how to use it. And you'd have to like train a whole version of programmers to use this new language.
turns.zh: 而且要让它们跟普通编程语言协作，真的非常非常难。原因之一是，如果你改动了那门语言，那么任何懂这些数据库的人都不会用了。你还得从头培训一整代程序员去用这门新语言。

turns.en: But now we're actually seeing databases come out, which are entirely new way of thinking about databases. It's a way better properties. They don't really have to train anybody because the agents already know how to do it. I think these things are path dependent, like some sectors, a new entrance is going to come and change it.
turns.zh: 但现在我们真的看到一些数据库出来了，它们是完全全新的思考数据库的方式，有更好的属性。它们几乎不用培训任何人，因为智能体早就知道该怎么做了。我觉得这些事情是有路径依赖（path dependent）的，有些板块会有新进入者来把它改掉。

turns.en: Like databases, OLTP may look entirely different in five years. And some, the incumbent may figure it out and be like, hey, listen, we're just going to add a few things. Networking, of course, which is this I did my PhD in networking. So it's an area of special interest. I guess it's been so sleepy and boring for the last 15 years.
turns.zh: 比如数据库、OLTP，五年后可能看起来完全不一样。而有些板块，在位者（incumbent）可能自己想明白，说，嘿，听着，我们只要加几样东西就行。网络（networking）当然也是——我做的是网络方向的博士（PhD），所以这是我特别感兴趣的一块。我猜过去十五年它一直太沉闷、太无聊了。

turns.en: And now because these clusters that we're building are so large. And they've got like such rigid performance constraints. We're seeing net new networking companies come out for the first time since Arista using changes in the materials used to build them. You were seeing optical come up.
turns.zh: 而现在，因为我们在搭建的这些集群如此庞大，而且有那么刚性的性能约束，我们看到自 Arista 以来第一批全新的网络公司冒了出来，用的是构建它们所用材料上的变化。你会看到光学（optical）在兴起。

turns.en: And so there's a lot of interesting stuff in networking. Compute the whole notion of what are the abstractions to run in the agent on? Is it like a container? Is it a VM? Is it a durable workflow? Something like temporal? That is changing.
turns.zh: 所以网络领域有很多有意思的东西。计算（compute）方面，『要在什么抽象之上运行一个智能体』这个整体概念——是容器（container）？是虚拟机（VM）？是像 Temporal 那样的持久化工作流（durable workflow）？这个正在变。

turns.en: But I do think we're at a point of maximum disruption where many points of the infrastructure stack can be rebuilt. Could we spend a few minutes on models? The traffic S1 came out this week. Obviously a beautiful view into the business itself.
turns.zh: 但我确实觉得我们正处在一个颠覆最大化的节点，基础设施栈上的很多环节都能被重建。我们能不能花几分钟聊聊模型？Anthropic 的 S-1 这周出来了，显然给了你一个看清这门生意本身的漂亮视角。

turns.en: But I'm actually more interested because the infrastructure stuff in what you think about just the state of these things today. I'm interested in all the debates. Close versus open. The public frontier versus the private frontier that the companies keep for themselves. Movement of talent. Opportunities.
turns.zh: 但其实我更感兴趣的，恰恰是基础设施那一块——你怎么看这些东西今天的状态。我对所有的争论都感兴趣。闭源对开源。公开的前沿（public frontier）对私有的前沿（private frontier），也就是公司留给自己用的那部分。人才的流动。机会。

turns.en: Things that don't exist that should. Whatever's on your mind about these things and how you see them evolving. I'm fascinated to hear. So I think the biggest question is is what happens if and when the market slows down? Because I think we've got three years of data of what happens in the existing very big fast growing market.
turns.zh: 那些还不存在、却应该存在的东西。关于这些东西你脑子里想的任何东西，以及你怎么看它们的演化，我都特别想听。所以我觉得最大的问题是，如果市场放缓——以及当它放缓时——会发生什么？因为我们已经有三年的数据，能看到在这个现存的、非常大、快速增长的市场里会发生什么。

turns.en: And like what happens there is being on the frontier means you've got tremendous pricing power. Even if you're just an epsilon better than the next guy, you've got tremendous pricing power. There's no demand problem. You've got basically infinite demand.
turns.zh: 在那里发生的情况是，处在前沿（frontier）意味着你有巨大的定价权。哪怕你只比下一个人强那么一丁点（epsilon），你也有巨大的定价权。不存在需求问题，你基本上有无限的需求。

turns.en: And so these frontier models that are the best tend to get 80% plus of the market dollar weighted. And that's happened for three years. But you can argue the reason that's happening is because we've not saturated the market at all. And people don't want the smartest thing.
turns.zh: 所以这些最好的前沿模型，往往会拿走按金额加权 80% 以上的市场份额。这种情况已经持续了三年。但你可以论证说，之所以会这样，是因为我们根本还没让市场饱和，而且人们要的就是最聪明的东西。

turns.en: And so then under that view, there's nothing structural is going to change as long as the market's growing. And you could argue this is going to go on for quite a while because what is a penetration point? 1% or something like that. They say 3% of the enterprise. But actually from budget wise, it's like 1% or less.
turns.zh: 所以在那种视角下，只要市场在增长，结构上就没有什么会变。你还可以论证说，这种情况会持续相当长的时间，因为渗透率才多少？1% 左右吧。他们说是企业里的 3%，但从预算角度看，其实是 1% 甚至更低。

turns.en: And so there's just a lot to grow given how useful the technology is. The more interesting question to me is what happens if the market starts to saturate in pockets? So if that happens, things shift to open source. Will you lose pricing power on the frontier?
turns.zh: 所以考虑到这项技术有多有用，还有巨大的增长空间。对我来说更有意思的问题是，如果市场在某些局部开始饱和，会发生什么？如果真发生，东西会转向开源（open source）。你会不会在前沿上失去定价权？

turns.en: One thing that we don't really do a good job of accounting for when we model out the numbers for these companies is what happens if you invest in a model and then you don't get the next model out really quickly? Let's assume that anthropic stumbles and they don't release the model for six months.
turns.zh: 有一件事我们在给这些公司建模、算数字时做得并不好，就是：如果你投了一个模型，然后你没能很快把下一个模型推出来，会发生什么？我们就假设 Anthropic 绊了一跤，六个月都没发布新模型。

turns.en: What is the lifespan that you think of the previous model? A very short period of time. It's very, very short, which is entirely different than we've ever had in software. And software we've always assumed some long tail. But it turns out what happens if you put out the soda model and everybody loves it, then something internal happens.
turns.zh: 你觉得上一个模型的寿命有多长？很短的一段时间。非常非常短，这跟我们在软件里历来拥有的东西完全不同。在软件里，我们总是假设会有某种长尾（long tail）。但结果是，如果你推出了 Sonnet 那个模型，人人都爱它，然后内部出了点事。

turns.en: I don't know what's regulatory. I don't know if it's technical. I don't know if it's a bridge, whatever. And then you slip three months, right? turns.zh: 我不知道是监管原因，是技术原因，还是要做个过渡版本（bridge）什么的。然后你延误了三个月，对吧？很有可能你就把整个市场都丢了。以我的经验，我看过很多这类模型公司的模型曲线图，都是从路演材料里来的——

turns.en: I would say the lifespan of a model is three to six months. So that means you have to release the next model. So again, for this conversation, I think it's a very interesting conversation. We should tease it apart. What happens if the market continues to grow and doesn't saturate? I think we already know.
turns.zh: 我会说，一个模型的寿命是三到六个月。所以这意味着你必须发布下一个模型。所以再说一次，对于这场对话，我觉得这是个非常有意思的话题，我们应该把它拆开来看。如果市场继续增长、不饱和，会发生什么？我觉得我们已经知道了。

turns.en: Because if three years of data, and it just means the frontier wins, and they do a great job and they create great models. Then what happens if either the use case is saturating, you don't need more intelligence, or the market starts slowing down for another reason. Nobody knows the answer to that.
turns.zh: 因为有三年的数据，它就意味着前沿会赢，他们做得很棒，创造出很好的模型。那么，如果是用例在饱和——你不再需要更多智能——或者市场因为别的原因开始放缓，又会发生什么？没人知道答案。

turns.en: I think there's a very real world where the value comes crashing back down into open source. And we'll see a shift that we've never seen, because software has always had a long tail of attention. On this trip, I've been asking a lot of people what percent of software coding tasks are already saturated,
turns.zh: 我觉得有一个非常现实的世界，就是价值会轰然回落到开源里去。我们会看到一种前所未见的转变，因为软件历来都有注意力的长尾。这一路上我一直在问很多人，软件编程任务里已经有百分之多少被饱和了，

turns.en: and the typical answer is very, very high percentage. That's been the biggest market. And yet, it still seems like people are spending like crazy on frontier tokens to do coding, which it seemed a little at odds. Like if I can do it with a six-month-old model or something that's vastly cheaper. Well, these are two different statements.
turns.zh: 而典型的答案是，非常非常高的百分比。那一直是最大的市场。可即便如此，人们似乎还是在为做编程而疯狂地烧前沿 token，这看起来有点自相矛盾。就像，如果我用一个六个月前的模型、或者某种便宜得多的东西就能搞定。嗯，这是两个不同的说法。

turns.en: This is a great thing to dig in on, but we need to be very careful. So statement number one is, I am not using more tokens. I have enough tokens. I've automated 95% already, so I can't automate anyone. And I think that we're getting pretty close to that. Comet number two is, therefore, I can use a cheaper model,
turns.zh: 这是个很值得深挖的点，但我们得非常小心。所以，说法一是：我没有在用更多 token，我已经有足够的 token 了，我已经自动化了 95%，没法再自动化更多了。我觉得我们正在相当接近这个状态。说法二是：因此，我可以用一个更便宜的模型——

turns.en: does not follow from Comet number one. So if you and I are competing startups, we've got Martin startup and Patrick startup, right? So we've got competing startups. And because we're in competitive equilibria, are you going to choose a donor model to compete with me?
turns.zh: ——这并不能从说法一推出来。所以如果你我是竞争性的初创公司，我们有 Martin 初创公司和 Patrick 初创公司，对吧？所以我们是互相竞争的初创公司。而因为我们处在竞争均衡里，你会选一个更笨的模型来跟我竞争吗？

turns.en: In competitive equilibria, you would always pay ten times more for the smartest model. Yeah, always, always, always. So there's this very open question of, will you saturate tasks so that you don't need a smarter model? And I think it's very hard to do that in a Darwinistic economic equilibria. When you're actually competing.
turns.zh: 在竞争均衡里，你总会愿意为最聪明的模型多付十倍的钱。是的，永远、永远、永远。所以这就有一个非常开放的问题：你会不会把任务饱和到不再需要更聪明模型的地步？我觉得在一个达尔文式的经济均衡里，当你真的在竞争时，这非常难做到。

turns.en: It's some of them may, but I think at the end of the day, it's about, can you get software out faster? Can you make it better and can you compete in a marketplace? And that will necessarily push you to the more intelligent thing. No, that said, clearly things will slow down because you're actually not spending more tokens.
turns.zh: 其中一些也许会，但我觉得归根结底，关键是：你能不能更快地把软件推出去？你能不能把它做得更好？你能不能在市场上竞争？而这些必然会把你推向更智能的那个东西。话虽如此，显然增速会放缓，因为你其实并没有花更多 token。

turns.en: And so either you have to increase prices, or you're going to have to go broad. But in my experience, the pricing is maintained, for sure. And because of the competitive equilibria, like you'll always want the smartest thing. And then we're just seeing a broadening use of these outside of code, general knowledge work.
turns.zh: 所以你要么得提价，要么就得走宽（go broad）。但以我的经验，定价是稳住了，绝对稳住了。而且因为竞争均衡，你总会想要最聪明的东西。然后我们就看到这些模型在代码之外、在通用知识工作（general knowledge work）里的使用在变宽。

turns.zh: 我只是觉得，我们被自己对『软件能做什么』的先入之见束缚得太死，以致于人们没在做这么多这类事情。我再给你举个例子。你知道，它能跟 Fei-Fei 的 World Labs 协作，那是家很棒的公司。我在那件事里、在他们做的事情里意识到的一点是，他们创造了一个模型，

turns.zh: 想象一下《千与千寻》（Spirited Away）在跑，你戴上 VR 眼镜走进去，你就在那里了。你看过《不眠之夜》（Sleep No More）那种沉浸式演出吗？我去看过。为什么不能有一个 VR 版的《不眠之夜》，让你走进去，整个剧情就在你身边上演？

turns.en: And like just for those that are listening sleep no more as an immersive play, which is three hours it was in this three story hotel or something like that building in New York and you're like running around trying to figure out and like hamlet is being played out or whatever. We're starting to realize how powerful this stuff is.
turns.zh: 给正在听的人解释一下，《不眠之夜》是一部沉浸式戏剧，长达三小时，当时是在纽约一栋三层楼的酒店之类的建筑里，你在里面到处跑、试图搞明白剧情，而《哈姆雷特》（Hamlet）之类就在你身边上演。我们开始意识到这些东西有多强大。

turns.en: A lot of these tropes and visions of the future from the 50s and 60s we can actually make. And I just think that the biggest constraint is no longer the tech. It's literally our creativity. And it's just because we've been beaten down by 30 years of software being a shit.
turns.zh: 很多来自五、六十年代的关于未来的桥段和想象，我们其实真的能造出来。我只是觉得，最大的约束已经不再是技术，而实实在在是我们的创造力。而这只是因为我们被『三十年软件都很烂』这件事给磨得没脾气了。

turns.en: I mean let's be honest software has sucked technology has been hard to use. Old people hate it. It's most often broken and now we're actually in a point where the stuff could actually start working. And so for me it's like I'm so excited for what this brings.
turns.zh: 我是说，老实讲，软件一直很烂，技术一直很难用，老年人讨厌它，它还老是坏掉。而现在我们其实正处在一个节点，这些东西可能真的开始能用了。所以对我来说，我为它将带来的东西感到无比兴奋。

turns.en: It's tempting to say you could just freeze the models and their current capability and still get all of what you described. So there's like a diffusion question I'd like to explore. Before we do that, what if anything do you think is missing from the models? Like how do you hope or wish or dream that the models themselves?
turns.zh: 很容易说，你完全可以把模型冻结在它们当前的能力上，仍然能得到你描述的那一切。所以有一个关于扩散（diffusion）的问题我想探讨一下。在那之前，你觉得模型现在缺了什么，如果有的话？你希望、期待、梦想模型本身变成什么样？

turns.en: So I think and I think you step back and you look at like what we know as an industry. The current tech stack anything that's digital with enough capital you can solve. And the reason is is because anything you can simulate on the computer, you can create RL environments for whether that's 3D using blender,
turns.zh: 我觉得，你退一步看我们作为一个行业所知道的东西——当前的技术栈里，任何数字化的东西，只要有足够的资本，你都能解决。原因是，任何你能在计算机上模拟的东西，你都能为它创建强化学习（RL）环境，不管是用 Blender 做 3D，

turns.en: whether that's general application use of a computer, whether it's code. You know, I have talked about this before. I think when it's all said and done, it's interesting to think about AI. The meta thing is that like you can take a money kid in and you can point it at a problem and it will solve that problem.
turns.zh: 不管是对计算机的通用应用操作，还是代码。你知道，我以前也谈过这个。我觉得当一切尘埃落定，关于 AI 那个元层面（meta）有意思的地方在于：你可以拿一笔钱，把它对准一个问题，它就会去解决那个问题。

turns.en: Like maybe it's expensive and at least you can solve it in the past. You'd be like blocked and engineering and you'd die. Now you can actually just direct money at problems and solve these problems. So I feel very confident saying anything in the digital world
turns.zh: 也许它很贵，但至少你能解决它。过去你会在工程上卡死，然后就完蛋了。现在你真的可以拿钱直接砸向问题、把问题解决掉。所以我非常有信心地说，数字世界里的任何东西——

turns.en: because you can create an environment and you can RL it and you can train on it, we can solve. So I just feel very comfortable. Anything you do with a computer and I will be able to do. Maybe it doesn't do it now, but like you can just see that path happening. What I don't know is does the same thing apply to physical universe?
turns.zh: ——因为你能创建一个环境，能用 RL 去训练它、在它上面训练，我们都能解决。所以我感到非常踏实：任何你用计算机能做的事，AI 都将能做。也许它现在还做不到，但你就是能看到那条路径正在发生。我不知道的是，同样的规律适不适用于物理宇宙。

turns.en: For sure you could set up a lab to like next speakers or whatever, you know, to do that. But like are the scaling curves the same? Is the distribution the same? So anything to do with robotics and the physical world and science and medicine, I have no idea if it follows the same laws. And so I think that's still an unlock.
turns.zh: 当然你可以搭一个实验室之类的去做那个。但那些扩展曲线（scaling curves）是一样的吗？分布是一样的吗？所以任何跟机器人（robotics）、物理世界、科学、医学有关的东西，我完全不知道它是否遵循同样的规律。所以我觉得那还是一个有待解锁的东西。

turns.en: But I feel very comfortable that the current digital side is done. How have you processed all this interesting security stuff? Breaches a vertical breach apocalypse. It's obvious that we're like entering a very interesting era in cyber. What do you make of all this? I lived through on the ground with formal studies in security.
turns.zh: 但我对当前数字这一侧已经搞定这件事，感到非常踏实。你是怎么消化所有这些有意思的安全话题的？各种数据泄露、某个垂直领域的泄露、末日级的泄露。显然我们正在进入一个网络安全（cyber）上非常有意思的时代。你怎么看这一切？我可是有安全方向的正规学术训练、亲身经历过这些的。

turns.en: I lived through the internet and it was way worse than this. Like by this time with the internet, we had worms and it cost billions of dollars of economic damage. We've taken out critical infrastructure. Remember Windows 95? No, I remember. Okay. Remember Windows 95? Just barely.
turns.zh: 我经历过互联网时代，那时候比现在糟糕多了。到互联网的这个时候，我们已经有了蠕虫病毒（worms），造成了数十亿美元的经济损失。我们干掉过关键基础设施。还记得 Windows 95 吗？不，我记得。好吧。还记得 Windows 95 吗？勉强记得。

turns.en: So it used to be that if you took Windows 95 and you installed it and it was connected to the internet, before the installer was done, it'd be infected. It's been taken away. It's not a joke, right? So like you do need to have time to patch it. It was so chaotic and there was so much mayhem.
turns.zh: 过去是这样的，如果你拿 Windows 95 装上、连到互联网，安装程序还没跑完，它就已经被感染了。它就被攻陷了。这不是开玩笑，对吧？所以你确实需要有时间去打补丁（patch）。那时候太混乱了，一片狼藉。

turns.en: And this is what happens every time you've got a new technology that changes the nature of how we run computers in the security posture. And we're definitely dealing with another one of those moments. And so I think we can look to what happened with the internet, which is like there's a few years of mayhem.
turns.zh: 每次你有一项新技术改变了我们运行计算机的方式和安全态势（security posture），都会发生这种事。而我们现在肯定又在应对这样的时刻之一。所以我觉得我们可以参照互联网当时发生的情况，也就是会有几年的混乱期。

turns.en: You do have breaches that cause real issues and then the industry evolves. And normally the way you think about security is like, well, the good guys be able to spend more money to the bad guys. If the answer is yes, which is typically the case, you will come up with a technical solution. And I think that will be the case here.
turns.zh: 你确实会遇到造成真实问题的数据泄露，然后这个行业就会进化。通常你思考安全的方式是，嗯，好人能不能比坏人花更多的钱？如果答案是能——通常就是能——你就会想出一个技术方案。我觉得这次也会是这样。

turns.en: And you're already starting to see it. These vulnerabilities that you see showing up, this is good. That means that somebody used the model to make things safer by pointing out the vulnerabilities. I think this is going exactly like you would expect it to go.
turns.zh: 而且你已经开始在看到它了。这些冒出来的漏洞，这是好事。那意味着有人用模型指出了这些漏洞，从而让东西更安全。我觉得这一切正完全按你会预期的方式在走。

turns.en: But I think the net impact that software will be much more secure because AI is also securing it. Can you talk about capital? There's very interesting things happening in capital markets. There's clearly lots of demand destruction happening.
turns.zh: 但我认为净影响是，软件会安全得多，因为 AI 也在保护它。你能谈谈资本吗？资本市场上正在发生一些非常有意思的事。显然有大量的需求破坏（demand destruction）在发生。

turns.en: We're not funding things that we would have in a different environment because the cost of capital to fund them is too high. And the cost is rising because the returns are so high on anything AI. I was like at this company this morning where if you and I had seen the deck five years ago,
turns.zh: 有些东西我们不再去投了，换在别的环境下我们本来会投，因为给它们融资的资本成本太高了。而成本在上升，是因为任何跟 AI 沾边的东西回报都太高了。我今天早上还在一家公司，如果你我五年前看到那份路演材料，

turns.en: it was an amazing software business and we should fund it. And now it seems to pale in comparison to other things that we could put our capital to. The capital itself feels like this interesting variable in this whole equation as a constraint. I'm curious how that feels to you.
turns.zh: 它是一门了不起的软件生意，我们该投。可现在，跟我们能把资本投向的其他东西一比，它就相形见绌了。资本本身，感觉像是这整个等式里一个很有意思的变量，一个约束。我很好奇这对你来说是什么感受。

turns.en: I sit on the boards with a lot of great companies that have the problem that you have. It's profitable, growing, 40, 50, 60 percent at scale, 300, 400, 500 million in ARR. What do those companies do? You can't really IPO because they're sub-scale, but they're great companies. And I think about my own personal portfolio.
turns.zh: 我在很多了不起的公司的董事会里，它们都有你说的那个问题。公司是盈利的、在规模化下以 40%、50%、60% 增长，ARR 有三亿、四亿、五亿美元。这些公司该怎么办？你没法真的 IPO，因为它们规模还不够大，但它们是很棒的公司。我也会想我自己的个人投资组合。

turns.en: I'm like whatever, I'm in muni bombs, man. I'd rather be in these companies, right? And so I think that everybody would be happy with an asset that grows 40 percent. Like you would be happy with your personal money being in there. If you can't see it. And so I still think these are very good companies. I feel it's more a question again.
turns.zh: 我就想，管它呢，我买的是市政债（munis），老兄。我宁愿投这些公司，对吧？所以我觉得，人人都会乐意拥有一个以 40% 增长的资产。如果是你自己的钱，你也会乐意放进去，前提是你买得到。所以我仍然觉得这些是非常好的公司。我觉得这更多又是一个问题。

turns.en: This is my naivety of not understanding this of like, are we going to see a shift in the market so that people can get exposure to this asset class? Because I think a risk profile is very, very different today. Nobody knows what's going to happen to AI when the market slows down. Nobody knows. It could be easy coming, easy go.
turns.zh: 这是我不懂这方面的天真之处——我们会不会看到市场发生一种转变，让人们能够接触到这一类资产？因为我觉得今天的风险画像（risk profile）非常非常不同。没人知道市场放缓时 AI 会怎样。没人知道。它可能是来得快去得也快。

turns.en: It could keep going forever. Like nobody really knows. And so the only free lunch I've ever seen in investing is diversification. And I would love to personally have one ask it. A best kit that includes these slower growing, but these assets that don't disappear
turns.zh: 它也可能永远涨下去。就是没人真的知道。所以我在投资里见过的唯一免费午餐（free lunch），就是分散化（diversification）。而我个人非常想有一个资产组合包（asset kit），一个包含这些增长较慢、但不会消失的资产的组合包。

turns.en: are most of the ones though that are in your mind extremely subjected to this disruption risk. There's lots of companies with that rough profile which seem terrifying in the face of how easy it's going to be to create software. I've been in for a guy. So for me, more software means you need more info. We don't vibe code databases yet.
turns.zh: 不过，你心里想的那些公司，大多数是不是都极度暴露在这种颠覆风险之下？有很多具备那种画像的公司，在『创造软件将变得多么容易』面前，看起来是挺吓人的。对我来说，更多的软件意味着你需要更多的基础设施。我们还没到 vibe code 数据库的地步。

turns.en: Like you do a very data like Snowflake be a well known example of kind of what you're talking about. Yeah, it's a great example. It's not just building it. It's really hard to have the long tailed features, the long tailed performance tweaks to actually operate these things is really, really tough.
turns.zh: 比如说一家非常数据密集的公司，像 Snowflake，会不会是你说的这种东西的一个知名例子？是啊，这是个很好的例子。这不只是把它搭出来。真正难的是那些长尾功能、长尾的性能调优，去实际运营这些东西，真的非常非常难。

turns.en: And so let's say that Snowflake is going 30% to 40% and the economics are good. Like I don't think that they're at any risk of being disrupted by AI. Maybe by data breaks, but that is like pre-AI type of thing. And so again, I'm very naive when it comes to these things. I'm a very simplistic thinker.
turns.zh: 所以假设 Snowflake 在以 30% 到 40% 增长，而且经济性不错。我不觉得它们有任何被 AI 颠覆的风险。也许会被 Databricks〔颠覆〕，但那是一种前 AI 时代的东西。所以再说一次，我在这些事情上很天真。我是个非常简单的思考者。

turns.en: My view is like I don't think AI is going to disrupt these. I think they are good businesses. I think more and more, the industry is going to want to wrap these up and get exposure. And I don't know what that looks like. It's kind of interesting. Like we're even seeing SPACs come back.
turns.zh: 我的观点是，我不觉得 AI 会颠覆这些。我觉得它们是好生意。我觉得这个行业会越来越想把这些打包起来、获得敞口。我也不知道那会长什么样。这挺有意思的。比如我们甚至看到 SPAC 在回归。

turns.en: I get a lot of calls now for companies that sit on the board out which are good companies where these SPACs are like, hey, listen, like we can make this stuff go public. So I think that the financial markets have to figure that out. There's a lot of companies that will be disrupted by AI. But there's a whole bunch that will not.
turns.zh: 我现在接到很多电话，是那些我坐在董事会里的好公司，这些 SPAC 说，嘿，听着，我们能把这些东西弄上市。所以我觉得金融市场得把这个想明白。有很多公司会被 AI 颠覆。但也有一大批不会。

turns.en: And I just think the market doesn't know what to do with them right now. Most meetings that you have around here, at least for me in the last, let's say, three months. Half the meeting is about compute. And that the product across categories just needs more compute that is available to accomplish its goals.
turns.zh: 而我就觉得，市场现在不知道该怎么对待它们。你在这边开的大多数会，至少对我来说，在过去——比方说——三个月里，一半的会都在谈算力（compute）。就是说，跨各类别的产品，只是需要更多可用的算力来达成它的目标。

turns.en: So there's another way of asking about the capital thing. You guys manage a ton of money. Everyone's deploying their funds at very fast paces. Each company that's working requires lots of capital. I'm trying to get a sense of the feel of how much capital itself is the constraint
turns.zh: 所以还有另一种问资本这件事的方式。你们管理着海量的钱。每个人都在以非常快的节奏部署他们的基金。每一家在运转的公司都需要大量资本。我想感受一下，资本本身在多大程度上是那个约束——

turns.en: that like if we just air dropped a trillion dollars more in all the funds, that would be a good thing. I said this before, but I've been a reiterate because it's so important. I really think the big disruption of AI is the fact that you can throw capital at problems.
turns.zh: 就是说，如果我们给所有基金凭空多撒一万亿美元，那会是件好事。我以前说过，但我要再强调一遍，因为这太重要了。我真的觉得，AI 最大的颠覆在于，你可以拿钱去砸向问题。

turns.en: In the history of tech, you haven't been able to do that because there's always an engineering problem, which just doesn't scale. The Mythical Man month is the Mythical Man month for the reason. Ten years ago, if I had five founders show up and asked for a billion dollars and I gave it to them, what would happen? It sits there.
turns.zh: 在科技史上，你一直没法这么干，因为总有一个工程问题，它就是没法规模化。《人月神话》（The Mythical Man-Month）之所以是《人月神话》，是有原因的。十年前，如果有五个创始人跑来要十亿美元，而我给了他们，会发生什么？钱就搁在那儿。

turns.en: Or they would detonate, right? They'd like hire a bunch of engineers and then you're really fucked. You can't throw capital at it. Can you explain the Mythical Man month? That's a very interesting idea. Yeah, so the Mythical Man month basically says that you can't increase the speed of engineering. It's like a natural law.
turns.zh: 或者他们会把它引爆，对吧？他们会去雇一大堆工程师，然后你就真的惨了。你没法拿钱去砸它。你能解释一下《人月神话》吗？那是个很有意思的概念。可以。《人月神话》基本上是说，你没法提高工程的速度。这就像一条自然法则。

turns.en: It's very sub-linear. It has to come with organizational communication. It's one of the conclusions. But the takeaway for those that are listening is that this comes from, I think Fred Brooks right under the 70s, which is basically like, you had these software projects and you wanted to get them out faster.
turns.zh: 它是极度亚线性的。它必须配合组织沟通。这是其中一个结论。但对正在听的人来说，要点是，这出自——我想是 Fred Brooks，在七十年代——基本上就是说，你有这些软件项目，你想更快地把它们做出来。

turns.en: And so they would throw more people at and then it would go slower. Engineering has always been this bottleneck. And in my experiences, and I had my own startup, I did it for ten years, right? It ended up being a very large business. This is totally true. You can't scale engineering.
turns.zh: 于是他们就往里面塞更多人，然后进度反而更慢了。工程一直是这个瓶颈。以我的经验——我自己创业过，干了十年，对吧？它最后变成了一门非常大的生意。这一点千真万确：你没法规模化工程。

turns.en: And to me, the biggest shifts, like we step back like industrial revolution level shift with AI is, I can take 20 people and I can give them a billion dollars and they can use that. Now, do they make 500 million from that billion or two billion? I have no idea.
turns.zh: 而对我来说，最大的转变——我们退一步看，这是工业革命级别的转变——就是，我可以拿 20 个人，给他们十亿美元，他们能把这钱用起来。那他们能从这十亿里做出五亿，还是二十亿？我不知道。

turns.en: But the fact that you can productively use that money is so new and it's so interesting. And so at some level, the capital markets need to figure this out because they are taking this money and using it. And if you look at anthropic and opening eye, they've probably raised more money and aggregate
turns.zh: 但『你能有生产效力地把那笔钱用起来』这件事，是如此全新、如此有意思。所以在某种层面上，资本市场需要把这个想明白，因为他们正在拿这些钱、并用起来。如果你看 Anthropic 和 OpenAI，他们融到的钱加起来，可能比整个下游生态加起来还多，多出好几倍。

turns.en: than the entire downstream ecosystem combined by a factor of whatever. They are these mechanisms of turning money into growth. So that's one side. But there's another side which is the debt side, which is quite a bit different than the equity side, which is I do think that currently I'm not a growth investor, not a public markets guy.
turns.zh: 他们就是这些把钱变成增长的机制。所以这是一面。但还有另一面，就是债务那一侧，它跟股权那一侧相当不同。我确实觉得，目前——我不是成长期投资人，不是公开市场的人，

turns.en: I'm not a debt guy. But here's what I'm sitting on the ground. We're running out of available debt. And if you're the Norway pension fund, are you going to give debt to a random neo-cloud or buy T-bills? And I think that we're just at a point where you don't have enough money to go around.
turns.zh: 我也不是做债务的人。但以下是我在一线看到的情况：我们可用的债务正在耗尽。如果你是挪威养老基金，你会把债借给一家随便冒出来的新云（neo-cloud），还是去买国债（T-bills）？我觉得我们正处在一个钱不够分的节点。

turns.en: So it's going to prefer the investment-grade companies. And then those that are not investment-grade will have a harder time. So scale wins again. Scale will win. And then it'll be a harder time raising debt. If your business model requires you to raise debt, there's just not enough debt to go out.
turns.zh: 所以它会偏向那些投资级（investment-grade）的公司。然后那些不是投资级的，会更难。所以规模又一次胜出。规模会赢。然后如果你的商业模式需要你举债，你会更难融到债，因为根本没有足够的债务可放。

turns.en: So I know what you're talking about capital is in general capital. You're going to see a ton of liquidity. I think that that feels fine to me. The debt side, I don't know these markets, but I definitely know it's harder to get debt now.
turns.zh: 所以我明白你说的资本是什么意思——总的来说是资本。你会看到海量流动性。我觉得那没问题。债务那一侧，我不懂这些市场，但我确实知道现在更难拿到债了。

turns.en: And I think what this will mean, if we want to have smaller players around that are not IG, they get debt. They're going to need to prepay, which means their customers are going to need to prepay. So I think over time, this all kind of flows back to the availability of cash and capital. Because you do have limited amounts of debt.
turns.zh: 我觉得这将意味着，如果我们想让那些规模较小、不是投资级（IG）的玩家留在场里、拿到债务，他们就得预付款，也就意味着他们的客户得预付款。所以我觉得随着时间推移，这一切都会回流到现金和资本的可得性上。因为你确实只有有限量的债务。

turns.en: This reminds me to ask about neo-labs, neo-clouds, inference providers and companies. I don't know if you call these infrastructure or what part of the stack. Yeah, that's all those infrastructures. So if you take those categories in turn, there's lots of them. Lots of them have been funded. Very few of them are at scale.
turns.zh: 这提醒我去问问新实验室（neo-labs）、新云（neo-clouds）、推理提供商（inference providers）这些公司。我不知道你会把这些叫作基础设施，还是栈里的哪一部分。是的，那些全都是基础设施。所以如果你逐个看这些类别，它们有很多，很多都拿到了融资，但极少达到规模。

turns.en: I'm curious how you think this plays out. Like what roles they should and will play, what the market feels like. These things are growing so unbelievably fast in those cases. I'm very interested by these companies. I'm curious what you think of these categories. Well, let's put neo-labs aside.
turns.zh: 我很好奇你觉得这会怎么演变。就是它们应该、以及将会扮演什么角色，市场感觉如何。这些东西在这些情况下增长得快得难以置信。我对这些公司非常感兴趣。我很好奇你怎么看这些类别。嗯，我们先把新实验室放一边。

turns.en: Because I think that's the least we'll define of all of them. I included them to be clear because so many of them seem to be building their own... They're becoming neo-class. Like every pitch. So many pitches turn into some version of like we're building a token factory with some degree of vertical integration.
turns.zh: 因为我觉得那是它们所有里面定义最不清楚的。我把它们包括进来，说清楚一点，是因为它们中很多似乎在自建自己的……它们正在变成新云。就像每一份路演材料。太多路演都变成了某种版本的『我们在建一个带一定垂直整合的 token 工厂』。

turns.en: And some neo-labs are going all the way down to like buying land and power and all the way up through the token. You know what I mean? So there's this year... Yeah, I think so. In my world, that wouldn't be considered a neo-lab. That'd be it. Like all neo-clouds want to be token factories.
turns.zh: 而且有些新实验室一路往下走到买地、买电，一路往上走到 token。你懂我意思吗？所以有这么一种……是的，我觉得是。在我的世界里，那不会被算作新实验室。那就是〔新云〕。就像所有新云都想成为 token 工厂。

turns.en: That would view if like your output is like a token of an existing model architecture or something else. Yeah, you're a neo-cloud. Like all of them want to do that and they will all verticalize. The actual real limitation right now is hardware supply. That's not capital. It's not debt. That's the actual real limitation and power.
turns.zh: 那要看，如果你的产出是某个现有模型架构的 token 或别的什么。是的，你就是个新云。就像它们全都想干这个，而且它们都会垂直整合。当下真正的限制是硬件供应。那不是资本，不是债务。那才是真正的限制，还有电力。

turns.en: So neo-cloud to me is one that actually provides the physical infrastructure that ends at tokens. And so they can provide GPUs. They can provide fine-tuning services or they can provide tokens. But it's like I think of like a data center that actually has the GPUs in it. That's what a neo-cloud is to me.
turns.zh: 所以新云对我来说，是那种真正提供物理基础设施、终点落在 token 上的公司。所以它们可以提供 GPU，可以提供微调（fine-tuning）服务，或者可以提供 token。但我把它想成一个真的把 GPU 放在里面的数据中心。这就是新云对我的含义。

turns.en: A neo-lab to me is give me a billion dollars. We're going to come up with a new model architecture. I love a lot of these business plans are like if we solve ASI, that's our business model. Like literally like that. And by the way, to be fair, that's what open AI's original thesis was.
turns.zh: 新实验室对我来说是，给我十亿美元，我们要搞出一个新的模型架构。我很喜欢——很多这类商业计划就是，如果我们解决了 ASI（通用超级智能），那就是我们的商业模式。真的就是这样。而且顺便说一句，公平地讲，那正是 OpenAI 最初的论点。

turns.en: And to some extent, anthropics, which is like if you solve the intelligence problem, the business model part is easy. So that's to me a neo-lab. It's new architecture, model training and sometimes they'll buy their own infrastructure and buy their own GPUs. But like that's not what they're building towards or selling.
turns.zh: 在某种程度上，Anthropic 也是，就是说如果你解决了智能问题，商业模式那部分就简单了。所以那对我来说就是新实验室。它是新架构、模型训练，有时候他们会买自己的基础设施、买自己的 GPU。但那不是他们要构建或售卖的目标。

turns.en: The real constraint right now is power. It is chips. It is materials. With that sort of a limitation, 80% of these things are going to go to the scale providers. 20% are just going to be kind of hard to reach places, nitchy type places. Like I have the relationship with a random government that has the power. It was kind of funny.
turns.zh: 当下真正的约束是电力，是芯片，是材料。有这样的限制，这些东西里 80% 会流向规模化的提供商。20% 就只是一些比较难触达的地方、小众的地方。就像我跟某个掌握电力的随机政府有关系。这有点搞笑。

turns.en: I bet this company a GPU marketplace. That's what it does. But it's like the most low level version of it. And like many of their GPS converted chicken sheds. You know, like chicken coops where like people in farms are like finding ways to provide it. So the market is so large, there will always be a significant portion.
turns.zh: 我押注了一家做 GPU 市场（marketplace）的公司。它就是干这个的。但它是这事儿最底层的版本。就像他们很多 GPU 是改造鸡舍来的。你知道，就是鸡舍、鸡笼那种，农场上的人在想办法提供算力。所以这个市场太大了，永远会有相当大的一部分，

turns.en: That just doesn't make sense for the SpaceX's to do. Like SpaceX is not going to go and find out how to create a marketplace of chicken coop GPUs. And I think this is what ended up happening is the 20% is large enough to have a very wide fragment of the array of folks.
turns.zh: 是那些 SpaceX 级别的公司去做没意义的。就像 SpaceX 不会去研究怎么搭一个鸡舍 GPU 的市场。我觉得最终发生的情况是，那 20% 已经大到足以容纳一大批形形色色、非常分散的玩家。

turns.en: But then the 80% of the market are going to be these homogenous things like SpaceX. I heard this story recently that someone asked Larry Page how much of compute will be orbital. And he said five nines. And the reason was it's just physics. Eventually it's all going to be in space. The actual spacing actually pencils out.
turns.zh: 但接下来，80% 的市场会是这些同质的东西，像 SpaceX。我最近听到一个故事，有人问 Larry Page，未来会有多少算力在轨道上（orbital）。他说了五个九（five nines）。原因是，这就是物理。最终它全都会跑到太空里去。那个太空的账其实是算得过来的。

turns.en: But the reason it makes the most sense is just regulatory. Just because it skirts it. Yeah. There's 500 proposed legislations to stop data center building the United States alone, including Texas. Right. Like if you can't build a data center of Texas, I don't know what we're doing anymore.
turns.zh: 但它之所以最说得通，纯粹是监管原因。就是因为它绕开了监管。是的。光是美国，就有 500 项拟议中的立法要阻止数据中心建设，包括 Texas。对。就像，如果你连在 Texas 都建不了数据中心，我就不知道我们还在干嘛了。

turns.en: If that regulatory pressure continues and you actually can't break ground. And I've heard from many of the top data center people like it's very tough to break ground right now. Then either you go international or you go into space. You're coming on these software companies growing 60%.
turns.zh: 如果那种监管压力持续下去，你真的没法动工。而且我从很多顶尖的数据中心从业者那里听到，现在动工非常难。那么要么你走向国际，要么你走向太空。你正碰上这些以 60% 增长的软件公司。

turns.en: Reminds you to ask about prevailing valuations in the market. And as a productive investor that's focused on disruptive assets being created. Even if the disruptive asset is truly incredibly valuable and great. Every one of those has a price that will ruin the return of investing in it. If it's too high.
turns.zh: 这提醒我去问一问市场上流行的估值。而作为一个专注于『颠覆性资产被创造出来』的生产性投资人，即便那项颠覆性资产真的无比有价值、无比出色，它们每一个都有一个价格，如果太高，就会毁掉投资它的回报。

turns.en: So this is another one of my bugaboo's. I don't know how you can be a VC and not believe tech rates value, which is the first conversation. And now I'm going to have a second conversation, which is I don't know how you can be a VC and not believe markets are efficient. What are we doing?
turns.zh: 所以这又是我的一个执念（bugaboo）。我不知道你怎么能既做 VC、又不相信技术创造价值，这是第一个话题。现在我要讲第二个话题：我不知道你怎么能既做 VC、又不相信市场是有效的。我们到底在干嘛？

turns.en: Like recapitalists, you have to believe markets are efficient. I think private markets are very efficient. And private markets figure out the price. And so I just don't try and bet against the market. I think a lot of people think that private markets aren't efficient. And so you can find the deal and find the non consensus deal.
turns.zh: 就像，作为风险投资人，你必须相信市场是有效的。我觉得私募市场非常有效。私募市场会把价格定出来。所以我从不去跟市场对赌。我觉得很多人认为私募市场无效，所以你能找到那个交易、找到那个非共识的交易。

turns.en: And all of those deals are incredibly competitive. And I didn't win by looking for a deal or whatever. I pay the market price and maybe I'll get a little discount for negotiating or whatever. But I never really worry about that. And so as a productive investor, I just trust that the markets are actually pretty smart.
turns.zh: 而所有那些交易都竞争得极其激烈。我也不是靠去找某个交易之类的赢的。我付市场价，也许我会因为谈判之类拿到一点点折扣。但我从不真的为那个操心。所以作为一个生产性投资人，我就是相信市场其实相当聪明。

turns.en: And I trust that the markets will value it given risk adjusted. And I believe that my diligence reduces that risk for me. I don't do it on market value. Yeah, I'm not trying to find a better price. I'm just trying to find a less riskier asset.
turns.zh: 而且我相信，市场会在风险调整后给它估值。而我相信我的尽调为我降低了那份风险。我不是在市场价值上做文章。是的，我不是想找一个更好的价格。我只是想找一个风险更低的资产。

turns.en: Doesn't it fall though that then the approach would be to actually try to index the private markets? Like you just try to own literally the market weights of... Oh, I would love to, but you can't. I would love to. Of course, yeah, so this is right. So there's where this all lends to. And this is kind of how we think about investing.
turns.zh: 那这不就意味着，接下来的做法应该是真的去试图给私募市场做指数化（index）吗？就像你就去持有那些字面意义上的市场权重……哦，我太想了，但你做不到。我太想了。当然，是的，所以这就对了。所以这就是这一切引向的地方。这也差不多是我们思考投资的方式。

turns.en: Of course, if I can have a 10 decks of every competitive deal. Like literally my dream would be I get five percent... If that was a cognition when you buy cursor. I have every cup. I've got five percent of every competitive. Like I really believe private markets are super efficient. I do. And I think that the consensus is actually smart.
turns.zh: 当然，如果我能拿到每一个竞争性交易的 10%。字面意义上，我的梦想会是拿到 5%——比如那如果是 Cognition，当你买 Cursor 的时候。我拿到每一份，我拿到每一个竞争性交易的 5%。我是说，我真的相信私募市场超级有效，我真的这么认为。而且我觉得共识其实是聪明的。

turns.en: Because I'm a capitalist and I believe in markets. And so if I could have five percent of every competitive deal where you've got legit investors and it not be happy. But you simply cannot do that. You can't do that for competitive reasons. You can't do that for capacity reasons.
turns.zh: 因为我是个资本主义者，我相信市场。所以如果我能拿到每一个竞争性交易的 5%——那些有正经投资人参与的交易——我会乐坏了。但你根本做不到那样。出于竞争原因你做不到，出于容量原因你也做不到。

turns.en: As an investor, you have to come up with how do I not run the competitive bus hub? Even more importantly, how do I not run out of our ability to keep track and help these companies? Because I do take the boards. I do get very involved, very involved. That's just impractical.
turns.zh: 作为一个投资人，你必须想出：我怎么才能不把竞争性交易跑光？更重要的是，我怎么才能不耗尽我们持续跟进、帮助这些公司的能力？因为我确实进董事会，我确实深度参与，非常深度。那根本不现实。

turns.en: So the way that we think about it, which you've heard before, but all of a restated is... For every legitimate sector. And by that legitimate sector, we define it as there's good founders in it. Because we don't second guest founders. They're risking their futures and the opportunity costs in their family's wealth.
turns.zh: 所以我们思考它的方式——你以前听过，但我再重述一遍——是：对每一个正当的板块。而所谓正当板块，我们的定义是里面有好的创始人。因为我们不质疑创始人。他们在拿自己的未来、机会成本、以及家族的财富去冒险。

turns.en: Then it's a good sector. We do the work to try to side for every good sector, which is the top company. And that means you look at the team, you look at the tech. And you look at the monetization potential. You look at the market growth potential. You look at all of that stuff. And then we choose the best one.
turns.zh: 那它就是个好板块。我们下功夫，去为每一个好板块挑出那家最好的公司。这意味着你看团队、看技术、看变现潜力、看市场增长潜力，你看所有那些东西。然后我们选出最好的那个。

turns.en: And then we assume that the market is efficient. That's kind of the approach. It's kind of an index, but we're actually segmenting it by market. Sometimes we get it right, and sometimes we get it wrong. But that way you're indexing the interesting markets. Yeah, there's this thing in indexing called stratified sampling.
turns.zh: 然后我们假设市场是有效的。这差不多就是那套方法。它有点像做指数，但我们其实是按市场来分层的。有时候我们判断对，有时候判断错。但那样你就在给那些有意思的市场做指数化。是的，指数化里有个东西叫分层抽样（stratified sampling）。

turns.en: It's from my old quantitatively. But you can buy a small subset of the index. And have your tracking error to the index be very low. Because actually literally what you're describing is effectively stratified sampling. Get the exposure to the best biggest to whatever per category. And that will perform similar. Yeah, okay.
turns.zh: 那是出自我以前做量化（quant）的老本行。但你可以买入指数的一小部分，却让你对指数的跟踪误差（tracking error）非常低。因为实际上，字面意义上，你描述的正是分层抽样。拿到每个类别里最好、最大的那个的敞口，表现就会相近。是的，好的。

turns.en: I think venture capital early on. And I wasn't there. I just read the books. I think it believed that tech created value. I mean, often there was no business to evaluate. And I just don't see so much hand ringing about bubbles or this or that or the other thing. The market price is the market price.
turns.zh: 我觉得风险投资在早期——我不在场，我只是读那些书——它相信技术创造价值。我是说，那时候常常根本没有一门生意可供评估。而我也看不到那么多关于泡沫、这个那个的捶胸顿足。市场价就是市场价。

turns.en: To me, there's always this huge dissonance when I'm talking with other investors. They're always declining the bubbles, which nobody can ever predict. But definition everybody's calling it a bubble. It's probably not a bubble. Like it's almost a bubble like when everybody's investing. Because they think there's still upsides.
turns.zh: 对我来说，我跟其他投资人谈话时总有这种巨大的失调感。他们总是在宣称泡沫，而没人能预测泡沫。但按定义，如果人人都在喊它是泡沫，它大概就不是泡沫。就像，它几乎是个泡沫——当人人都在投的时候——因为他们觉得还有上行空间。

turns.en: And then they don't somehow think private markets are efficient. Remember, I got VC canceled because I'm like non-consisting investing is dangerous. I once on Twitter was like, hey, listen, I think it's dangerous to invest against consensus because basically there's fall on capital risk. And from saying that, many prominent VCs came out.
turns.zh: 然后他们又不知怎的不认为私募市场是有效的。记住，我被 VC 圈『取消』过，因为我说非共识投资是危险的。我曾经在 Twitter 上说，嘿，听着，我觉得逆着共识投资是危险的，因为基本上有本金全损的风险。就因为说了这话，很多知名 VC 站了出来。

turns.en: And they're like, oh, like all of these deals that we've done were non-consensus. And I think there's something very tied to the ego and the identity of investors that they have to believe that they can truffle hunt and find the non-consisting they're smarter than everybody else.
turns.zh: 他们说，哦，我们做过的所有这些交易都是非共识的。而我觉得，投资人身上有种东西跟自我（ego）和身份认同绑得很紧，他们必须相信自己能像刨松露一样挖出那些非共识的东西、相信自己比所有人都聪明。

turns.en: But I think the reality is, is certainly if you look at our portfolio, the ones that return money were actually very, very competitive in general. I just think these marks are actually quite efficient. I love the idea of market efficiency and private markets being one area that you disagreed with lots of well-known.
turns.zh: 但我觉得现实是，如果你看我们的投资组合，那些真正赚回钱的，一般来说其实都竞争得非常非常激烈。我就是觉得这些市场其实相当有效。我很喜欢『市场有效性』这个说法，也很喜欢私募市场是你在很多知名 VC 那里持异议的一个领域这件事。

turns.en: Yeah, apparently a whole lot. Really all of them. Are there any other areas like that where you feel especially alone? Yes. There's another one that drives me nuts. This is my last one I promise. Another thing that drives me nuts is this belief that if you put money in private markets it doesn't somehow grow the time of private markets.
turns.zh: 是的，显然跟一大票人意见相左。真的是所有那些人。还有没有别的领域，是你觉得自己特别孤立的？有。还有一个快把我逼疯的。这是我最后一个，我保证。另一件快把我逼疯的事，是这种信念：如果你把钱投进私募市场，它就不知怎的不会让私募市场的 TAM 增长。

turns.en: I love roll-off. I think he's fantastic. He's probably intelligent guy. He's a great board member. But he gave this talk. Do you remember that TechCrunch distributed many investors believe this? So this isn't to call for a lot because I was actually a huge fan of his but he was like, venture capital is not an asset class.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢 Roll-off。我觉得他非常出色。他大概是个很聪明的人。他是个很棒的董事会成员。但他做过一个演讲。你还记得那个 TechCrunch Disrupt 吗？很多投资人都信这一套。所以这不是要喷他——因为我其实一直是他的粉丝——但他当时说，风险投资不是一个资产类别。

turns.en: There's only 20 startups that matter. And that's it. If there's too much money going in, you've overfunded private markets. And to me, this is ludicrous. Capital creates opportunities and markets and value. And even though there is so much more money that has gone into private markets
turns.zh: 只有 20 家初创公司才重要。就这样。如果有太多钱涌进去，你就把私募市场过度融资了。而对我来说，这是荒谬的。资本创造机会、创造市场、创造价值。而且尽管在过去 20 年里

turns.en: in the last 20 years, the value in the private markets has kept pace. You've gotten massive private companies, tons of opportunities, very large exits. And so this zero sum thinking about private markets. So bizarre. We're venture investors. We create value. Tech creates value. If you put more money in it, it'll grow.
turns.zh: 有那么多钱涌进了私募市场，私募市场里的价值却跟上了步伐。你得到了巨型私募公司、大量机会、非常大的退出。所以这种对私募市场的零和（zero sum）思维，太离谱了。我们是风险投资人。我们创造价值。技术创造价值。如果你往里投更多钱，它会增长。

turns.en: And you will be surprised. And maybe you won't be surprised. But I've been very surprised how calm in this mindset is. I'm very often I'll talk to a pretty senior GP. turns.zh: 举个例子，你不会把我放进一家矿业公司的董事会。所以想想 2021 年，我们会有这些 PE 投资人。他们会投这些非常 PE 式的公司。我会跟这些人一起坐董事会。那简直就像把我放进一家矿业公司的董事会？是的。是的。

turns.en: Like trying to like reason about the company through like burn. Like you're going to be miserable here. Because all we do is burn cash for a long time. It's more like kind of the blending of the lines because private companies are a real asset class for late stage investors. A lot of this is just growing pains.
turns.zh: 就像试图通过烧钱率（burn）来推理这家公司。就像，你在这儿会很痛苦。因为我们所做的就是长时间地烧现金。这更像是界线在模糊，因为对后期投资人来说，私募公司是一类真实的资产。很多这只是成长的烦恼（growing pains）。

turns.en: Like how much larger do you think the market is now than it was 30 years ago? Thousand times? So of course, of course, the interest is going to have to mature around that. And of course, you're going to have to view it like a kind of later stage investor, of course. But I just think that there's this funny identity crisis
turns.zh: 就像，你觉得现在的市场比 30 年前大了多少？一千倍？所以当然，当然，围绕它的这套机制必然要成熟起来。而且当然，你将不得不像一个后期投资人那样去看待它，当然。但我就觉得，很多后期投资人身上有这么一种有意思的身份认同危机，

turns.en: with a lot of later stage investors who view the world that way just because they're in private markets and their VCs think that, for example, I would never invest in a late stage company. Like I don't think it goes here. Like I'm like, what would I do? I go there and tell you how to run a finance app. I just not me. So I think that's it.
turns.zh: 他们那样看世界，只是因为他们在私募市场里、他们是 VC，就认为——举个例子——我永远不会去投一家后期公司。就像，我不觉得那适合我。我会想，我去了能干嘛？我去那儿告诉你怎么运营一个金融 app 吗？那不适合我。所以我觉得就是这样。

turns.en: It's basically the encourage of traditional banking and traditional finance and venture, which absolutely belongs there. I just think sometimes it kind of reaches a little bit too low. And then you have these issues. You have these issues in M&A where they're like, whatever, let's run an auction and let's do all this other stuff.
turns.zh: 这基本上是传统银行、传统金融对风险投资的侵入，而它们绝对属于那里。我只是觉得，有时候它伸得有点太往下了。然后你就有了这些问题。你在 M&A 上有这些问题，他们会说，管它呢，我们来办一场拍卖，来做所有那些别的把戏。

turns.en: You have it in the operations of a company where like you're 20 people on the radio up burn or they're over rotating on metrics for disruptive technology. I just feel like we need to kind of bring back traditional productive VC for some subset of this and there's enough market for everyone.
turns.zh: 你在公司的运营上也有这些问题，比如你才 20 个人却在疯狂烧钱，或者他们在为颠覆性技术过度盯着那些指标。我就是觉得，我们需要为其中一部分把传统的生产性 VC 找回来，而且市场足够大，容得下每个人。

turns.en: Has anything changed about how when you meet somebody for the first time like if I came and watched 10 meetings in a week with you 10 years ago and you started? And then I came today and watched 10 meetings with you. Have you changed how you conduct your early interactions with founders? Yeah, a lot.
turns.zh: 有没有什么改变了——就是当你第一次见到某个人时的方式？就像，如果我来跟你一起在一周里看 10 场会，在 10 年前、你刚起步时；然后我今天再来跟你一起看 10 场会。你有没有改变你跟创始人进行早期互动的方式？有，改变很多。

turns.en: I mean, I think most investors go through this, especially when you come from the operating world. You have to learn how to listen as an investor. And then you also have to learn how to ask the questions that you really care about so that you can answer the questions to yourself. And it's a very delicate balance.
turns.zh: 我是说，我觉得大多数投资人都要经历这个过程，尤其是当你来自运营界的时候。你得学会作为一个投资人去倾听。然后你还得学会去问那些你真正在意的问题，好让你能自己回答那些问题。这是一个非常微妙的平衡。

turns.en: I do feel like a lot of meetings with founders tend to be pretty performative on both sides. Like you don't know what to ask. And so you'll be like, who's your competition? And then a lot of it is just asking questions for asking questions, say, but again, it doesn't actually inform your decision.
turns.zh: 我确实觉得，很多跟创始人的会，双方都倾向于相当表演性（performative）。就像你不知道该问什么。所以你会问，你的竞争对手是谁？然后很多就只是为了问而问，可它其实并不能给你的决策提供信息。

turns.en: And then especially if you're an operator, you'll hear something you disagree with. And you kind of want to fix that problem. But that's kind of not your job. I have learned, and I'm not perfect. But the primary job is just to listen. A founder will tell you what they believe. If you disagree, you disagree. But that's what they believe.
turns.zh: 然后尤其是如果你是个运营者，你会听到某个你不同意的东西。你就有点想去解决那个问题。但那有点不是你的活儿。我学到了——我并不完美——但首要的活儿就是倾听。一个创始人会告诉你他们相信什么。如果你不同意，你不同意就是了。但那就是他们所相信的。

turns.en: So often they'll say something like, well, but I would do it better and therefore like it's a good investment. It's truly an art. You have to make a decision based on that meeting. There's a lot of silly questions you could ask that are not really going to inform that decision. What if Amazon does that? What is OpenAI? Like, whatever.
turns.zh: 所以他们常常会说类似，嗯，但我会做得更好，因此这是笔好投资。这真的是一门艺术。你得基于那场会做一个决定。有很多愚蠢的问题你可以问，但它们其实不会给那个决定提供信息。如果 Amazon 也做那个怎么办？如果 OpenAI 呢？随便啦。

turns.en: You can answer that yourself. Maybe you can figure out how they think. But there are key questions that you really want to know. And kind of knowing which ones those are during the time of the meeting and getting those in is a hard thing to do. And I think I've really refined my ability to do that.
turns.zh: 那些你自己就能回答。也许你能借此摸清他们怎么想。但有一些关键问题是你真的很想知道的。而在开会的那段时间里，判断出哪些是关键问题、并把它们问进去，是件很难做到的事。而我觉得我真的磨练出了做这件事的能力。

turns.en: Maybe a fun place to close is just to ask what has you most excited? We've talked about lots of the magic of this new era of technology and things that weren't possible before bottlenecks that are now gone. I know all of that excites you. But if you had to just step all the way back and describe why this job is so incredibly fun right now
turns.zh: 也许一个有意思的收尾方式，就是问问什么最让你兴奋。我们已经聊了这个技术新时代的很多魔法，以及那些从前不可能、如今瓶颈消失的事情。我知道所有这些让你兴奋。但如果你不得不彻底退后一步，描述为什么这份工作现在如此难以置信地有趣，

turns.en: and why you're most excited. I have more and more of the belief that this is an industrial revolution level shift. And for me, the industrial revolution went from basically a zero sum world to like a non-zero sum where value is being created. And that new value is being created. And I think this is a very similar shift
turns.zh: 以及为什么你最兴奋。我越来越相信，这是一场工业革命级别的转变。而对我来说，工业革命是从一个基本零和的世界，走向一个非零和、价值被创造出来的世界。新的价值被创造出来。我觉得这是一场非常相似的转变，

turns.en: where before to solve problems, you had to solve very complex engineering problems which basically didn't scale or were very tough. And then you'd have to maintain them. And that's why all software has always sucked. It's basically being a capital problem. I don't know about the real world yet. I think we'll get there.
turns.zh: 在从前，要解决问题，你得去解决非常复杂的工程问题，而那些基本上没法规模化，或者非常艰难。然后你还得去维护它们。这就是为什么所有软件一直都很烂。它基本上变成了一个资本问题。现实世界我还不好说，我觉得我们会到那一步。

turns.en: But I think we've turned this into a capital resourcing problem. And we're capital allocators. And so I just feel like we're just in this very, very strategic position to help drive the future in a much, much more direct way than we ever have been before. Because I think this is a scale up capital game that causes that to happen.
turns.zh: 但我觉得我们已经把这件事变成了一个资本、资源的问题。而我们是资本配置者（capital allocators）。所以我就觉得，我们正处在一个非常非常有战略意义的位置上，能以一种比以往任何时候都直接得多的方式去帮助驱动未来。因为我觉得这是一场规模化的资本游戏，正是它促成了那件事。

turns.en: I don't believe private markets have limited time. I think they have unlimited time and the more money that goes into them, the more value that it would be created. So I just feel like we're in this very privileged position, very key to the innovation chain. And we're both very lucky to be here.
turns.zh: 我不相信私募市场有有限的容量。我觉得它们有无限的容量，而且投进去的钱越多，会被创造出来的价值就越多。所以我就觉得，我们正处在一个得天独厚的位置上，是创新链条里非常关键的一环。而我们俩都非常幸运能身处此地。
